sorular.konu: Why RAG: LLM limitations and the retrieval decision
sorular.soru: A student asks a chatbot about a school rule that changed last month. The bot gives the old rule. Which limit of an LLM explains this best?
secenekler: Limited context: the new rule is too long to fit in one prompt
Distraction: the key fact is hidden inside a very long prompt
Knowledge cutoff: its training data ends before the rule changed
Token cost: the model makes answers short to save money on tokens
sorular.aciklama: The model only knows its training data, so a rule that changed after that point is missing. Limited context is about how much text fits in one prompt, but here the bot was given no text about the new rule.

sorular.konu: RAG vs. Long Context vs. Fine-Tuning
sorular.soru: A company wants its bot to answer in a short, formal style. The facts it needs are general and stay the same. Which approach fits this goal best?
secenekler: Fine-tuning, because style is a behavior that the weights can learn
RAG, because fresh or private facts must be fetched for each question
Long context, because a few known documents can fit in the window
Continued pretraining, because the model needs a new domain or language
sorular.aciklama: Style and format are behavior, and new behavior is a job for fine-tuning. RAG is for fresh or private facts, but these facts are general and stable, so there is nothing new to fetch.

sorular.konu: RAG vs. Long Context vs. Fine-Tuning
sorular.soru: A bot is right when the key chunk comes first in the prompt. When the same chunk sits in the middle of many chunks, the bot often fails. Why?
secenekler: The reranker drops every chunk that is not placed at the very top
The prompt cache keeps only the first chunk, so the rest go unread
The context window is full, so the middle chunks are cut off first
The model tends to miss evidence in the middle of a long prompt
sorular.aciklama: Models tend to use the start and end of a long prompt best, and they often miss what sits in the middle. Nothing was cut off, because the chunk is still in the prompt, so the problem is attention and not space.

sorular.konu: RAG pipeline: offline indexing and online querying
sorular.soru: In a RAG prompt, each retrieved chunk gets a number in brackets. What is the main reason for this?
secenekler: The reranker can use the numbers to put the best chunk first
The answer can cite each chunk, so a reader can check every claim
The prompt cache can store each numbered chunk for later calls
The vector database can use the numbers to filter old chunks out
sorular.aciklama: With numbered chunks, the model can write a number after each claim, and a reader can open that source to check it. The reranker orders chunks by reading each one with the query, so it does not need any numbers.

sorular.soru: A team wants to index a FAQ page with many short questions and answers. Which way of chunking fits this page best?
secenekler: Blocks of equal length, so every chunk has the same number of tokens
Windows with a large overlap, so every answer is stored more than once
The whole page as one chunk, so no answer is ever split into two parts
One question with its answer per chunk, so each chunk is one full fact
sorular.aciklama: Splitting on the page's own structure keeps each question next to its answer, so one chunk holds one complete fact. Equal-length blocks ignore the text, so a cut can fall in the middle of an answer.

sorular.soru: A long article moves from topic to topic without any headings. Which chunking method can still cut it where the topic changes?
secenekler: Semantic chunking: it cuts where nearby sentences become less similar
Document-based chunking: it turns each section under a heading into a chunk
Recursive chunking: it splits by paragraph first, then by sentence
Sliding window: it cuts every few tokens and repeats some boundary text
sorular.aciklama: Semantic chunking compares the meaning of nearby sentences and cuts where it drops, which is where the topic changes. Document-based chunking needs headings or sections to follow, and this article has none.

sorular.konu: Embeddings, cosine similarity, and indexing hyperparameters
sorular.soru: A team puts each whole chapter into one chunk. Now search often misses small, specific facts. What is the most likely cause?
secenekler: Each fact loses its context, so the chunk means too little on its own
The overlap repeats too much text, so the index fills up with copies
Many topics blur into one vector, so no single fact stands out
The embedding size shrinks, so each vector can hold less meaning
sorular.aciklama: One vector for a whole chapter mixes many topics, so a question about one small fact does not match it well. Losing context is the problem of chunks that are too small, not of chunks that are too big.

sorular.konu: Dense, sparse, and hybrid retrieval; vector databases and ANN
sorular.soru: Many RAG systems run keyword search and semantic search together, then merge the two lists. What is the main reason for this?
secenekler: Keyword search finds the candidates, and semantic search then reranks all of them
Keyword search catches exact names, and semantic search catches similar meaning
Keyword search runs offline, and semantic search runs again for each question
Keyword search filters by date, and semantic search filters by user rights
sorular.aciklama: Keyword search is strong on exact names and numbers, and semantic search is strong when the same idea uses other words, so together they miss less. Reranking is a separate, later step, done by a model that reads the query and the chunk together.

sorular.konu: Dense, sparse, and hybrid retrieval; vector databases and ANN
sorular.soru: Vector databases often use approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search. What do they gain, and what do they give up?
secenekler: They gain a lot of speed and give up a little accuracy
They gain exact results and give up some storage space
They gain word matching and give up search by meaning
They gain shorter vectors and give up part of the meaning
sorular.aciklama: ANN searches only the part of the index closest to the query instead of every vector, so it is much faster and the top results are almost the same. It cannot promise exact results, because it trades a little accuracy for speed.

sorular.soru: One chunk says only 'Room: Main Hall'. A search for 'Where is the history exam?' misses it. How does Contextual Retrieval help?
secenekler: It writes a fake answer to the question and searches with that answer
It caches the whole document, so later calls can read the chunk faster
It joins each chunk with the next one, so every chunk becomes longer
It adds context from the full document, so the chunk mentions the exam
sorular.aciklama: Alone, the chunk has no words about the exam, so Contextual Retrieval adds a short note from the full document, such as 'History exam room: Main Hall'. Prompt caching only makes writing these notes cheaper, and it does not change what a chunk says.

sorular.soru: A system fetches many chunks, reranks them, and sends only the best few to the LLM. What is the goal of each part of this plan?
secenekler: Fetching many gives precision, and keeping few makes sure nothing is lost
Fetching many lowers the cost, and keeping few makes the search faster
Fetching many protects recall, and keeping few keeps the prompt focused
Fetching many fills the window, and keeping few protects the prompt cache
sorular.aciklama: A wide first search makes it less likely that a useful chunk is lost, and a short prompt helps the model use the best evidence. Saying that fetching many gives precision swaps the two goals, because precision comes from keeping only the best.

sorular.soru: Logs show that the correct chunk was in the prompt, near the top, but the answer was still wrong. Which part should the team fix first?
secenekler: Retrieval: chunking and hybrid search, since the search missed the chunk
Generation: the prompt rules and citations, since the model misread it
Ranking: a stronger reranker, since the chunk was placed too low to use
Indexing: a bigger embedding size, since the chunk's vector was too weak
sorular.aciklama: The right chunk reached the prompt near the top, so search and ranking did their job and the model misread it. A stronger reranker only reorders chunks, and this chunk was already near the top.

sorular.konu: Evaluation: retrieval metrics, golden set, correctness vs. faithfulness
sorular.soru: A team sets aside some golden-set questions and uses them only for testing, after all tuning is done. Why does it do this?
secenekler: To test if the system says 'I don't know' when it should
To give the LLM judge examples of good and bad answers
To see how real users write their questions in the logs
To get an honest score on questions the tuning never saw
sorular.aciklama: If you tune on every question, the score can look good only because the system fits those exact questions. Unanswerable rows test 'I don't know', which is a different job from keeping a fair test set.

sorular.konu: Evaluation: retrieval metrics, golden set, correctness vs. faithfulness
sorular.soru: An answer can be faithful to the retrieved context and still be wrong. Which case shows this?
secenekler: The retrieved chunk is outdated, and the answer repeats it exactly
The model ignores the chunk and answers from its old training data
The model joins two chunks and adds a date that neither chunk gives
The chunk has the right date, but the model writes a different one
sorular.aciklama: Faithful means every claim is supported by the retrieved context, and correct means it matches the truth. An outdated chunk can be followed perfectly and still be wrong, while answering from memory is not faithful at all.

sorular.konu: Advanced RAG: HyDE, CRAG, Multi-hop, GraphRAG, Agentic and Multimodal RAG
sorular.soru: What does agentic RAG add to a basic RAG system?
secenekler: It writes a fake answer first and then searches with that answer
It builds a graph of entities and follows the links between them
It checks if the context is enough and, if not, keeps calling tools
It grades each document and keeps only the useful parts of each one
sorular.aciklama: Agentic RAG adds a loop: when the retrieved context is not enough, an agent plans a step, calls a tool such as web search or SQL, and reads the result. Grading documents and keeping only the useful parts is what CRAG does.

sorular.konu: Advanced RAG: HyDE, CRAG, Multi-hop, GraphRAG, Agentic and Multimodal RAG
sorular.soru: HyDE asks the LLM to write a fake answer, then searches with that text instead of the short question. Why can this find better documents?
secenekler: A fake answer is graded first, so wrong documents are dropped early
A fake answer looks more like real documents than a short question
A fake answer is kept in the prompt, so the LLM has more evidence
A fake answer has exact names, so keyword search can match each one
sorular.aciklama: Documents are written like answers, so the embedding of a fake answer lands closer to them than the embedding of a short question. The fake text is thrown away after the search, so it never becomes evidence in the prompt.

sorular.konu: RAG security, knowledge conflicts, and application-specific design
sorular.soru: The only retrieved chunk gives this year's exam date, but the bot answers with last year's date from its training. What is happening, and what helps?
secenekler: Knowledge conflict: tell the model to prefer the newer, official context
Prompt injection: treat the retrieved text as data and never as orders
Retrieval miss: improve chunking and search so the date can be found
Lost in the middle: move the chunk with the date to the end of the prompt
sorular.aciklama: The model's memory and the retrieved evidence disagree, and memory won, so tell the model to prefer the context and add dates as metadata. It is not a retrieval miss, because the new date did reach the prompt.

sorular.konu: RAG security, knowledge conflicts, and application-specific design
sorular.soru: A team wants the LLM to read every chunk and then follow a rule to hide salary data. Why is it safer to filter chunks by user permission first?
secenekler: Filtering raises recall, so each user gets more useful chunks back
Filtering blocks prompt injection hidden inside the salary files
Filtering keeps secrets out of the prompt, where rules alone can fail
Filtering trains the LLM, so it learns which files each user may see
sorular.aciklama: An LLM can still repeat a secret it has read, even when the prompt tells it not to, so the safe design removes the chunk before the prompt is built. Blocking prompt injection is a different defense, which treats retrieved text as data and not as orders.
